articles.title: The Representation Trap: How Minority Power Shapes Electoral Politics in India
articles.abstract: Liberal democracy requires that minority groups be represented in politics. This article argues that minority representation can also generate headwinds for political inclusion by dividing the minority group and consolidating the dominant group. I study the combination of these processes, termed the representation trap, through a mixed-methods examination of Muslims in India. Analyses of election results and an original survey of Hindu and Muslim voters show that electing a Muslim representative divides Muslim votes across an increased share of coethnic candidates and consolidates Hindu votes for the majoritarian party in the subsequent election. Qualitative evidence and a vignette experiment trace these patterns to two mechanisms: sub-identity activation among Muslims and super-ordinate identity mobilization among Hindus. By showing how representation restructures elite and voter behavior within both minority and dominant groups, the article highlights the dynamic nature of ethnic politics and complicates the view of minorities as politically unified.

articles.title: Crime and Participation
articles.authors: DAVID DOHERTY, G. AGUSTIN MARKARIAN, MENA WHALEN, DANA GARBARSKI
articles.abstract: Does exposure to crime mobilize or demobilize political participation? We report findings from a preregistered design, leveraging data from an original survey of 21 major U.S. cities and five waves of the Cooperative Election Study. We assess the relationships between direct victimization, local (ZCTA-level) crime rates, and perceived neighborhood safety and two outcomes: turnout (including validated turnout) and non-electoral participation. We find that direct victimization is significantly associated with more non-electoral engagement but lower turnout. The negative estimated effects of victimization on turnout exceed the magnitude of positive effects associated with common get-out-the-vote efforts. We find only limited evidence that crime rates are associated with participation. Perceived neighborhood safety is associated with higher rates of non-electoral, but not electoral, participation. Our findings offer new, comprehensive evidence on the relationship between crime exposure and political participation and illustrate the importance of distinguishing between types of exposure and forms of participation.

articles.title: When Can Clientelism Serve Democratic Ends? A Democratic Theory of Distributive Politics
articles.abstract: This article employs normative democratic theory to examine a counterintuitive suggestion raised repeatedly by empirical scholars of clientelism: namely, that practices of particularistic exchange might sometimes serve democratic ends. Certainly, most particularistic practices are widely agreed to undermine democracy, on both intrinsic and instrumental grounds. Yet some observers resist blanket condemnation—and in particular, many highlight the redeeming democratic virtues of certain practices that seem to facilitate collective organization among disempowered groups. Drawing on “realist” approaches to democratic theory, we vindicate this basic insight while clarifying its scope conditions. Countervailing power is a crucial democratic priority, and programmatic methods of promoting it sometimes face serious obstacles: as when clientelist practices are deeply entrenched, or incumbents capture the tools of programmatic competition. Under such conditions, we conclude, democracy-seeking leaders may justifiably employ particularistic practices to promote countervailing power—but only if they respect five constraints tethering them strictly to that goal.

articles.title: The Idea of a Counter-Structure: Rethinking Collective Action against Climate Injustice
articles.abstract: This article argues that addressing the structural injustices of climate change requires rethinking collective action. Disruptive and prefigurative politics are often treated as separate collective action repertoires, but I argue that a just energy transition requires that they work in tandem. To capture this interaction, I propose the idea of “counter-structural” collective action, in which disruptive protest creates windows of opportunity that prefigurative alternatives can then fill. Through analysis of two UK climate movements, Transition Towns (TTs) and Camps for Climate Action (CCA), I show how activists reconfigure structural elements to build new, carbon-free social and political forms. The theory of counter-structural action provides a framework for assessing the empirical cases. The cases, in turn, illustrate a broader conception of collective action that better reflects the social theory grounding structural injustice. Together, the theory and cases support the dual aims of climate justice: challenging fossil-fuel path dependence and advancing egalitarianism.

articles.title: Gender Bias in Bribe Solicitation: Evidence From Firm–State Interactions
articles.authors: Daniela Donno, Andreas Kern, Bernhard Reinsberg, Juliette Taylor
articles.abstract: Previous research has shown that women-led businesses are less likely to bribe officials to bypass administrative burdens, assuming that this is because women are less susceptible to corruption. We uncover an additional mechanism that focuses on the beliefs and practices of corrupt officials: bureaucrats underestimate women as entrepreneurs and hence reduce their demand for bribes from women-led enterprises. We confirm these expectations using the World Bank Enterprise Survey on a sample of 109,929 firms in 149 countries from 2006 to 2022. Split-sample analyses focusing on gender-unequal societies further support our hypothesized mechanism and suggest tentatively that sexual corruption may substitute for bribery as female-led businesses interact with public sector officials. The results have important implications for understanding the drivers of corruption, notably its gendered dimension and the role of women’s leadership as an engine for integrity, though for perhaps unexpected reasons.

articles.title: Explaining Military Defections in Democracies: The Impact of Executive Self-Coups
articles.abstract: Militaries sometimes defect during protests, including in democracies. The scholarship on defections in nondemocracies highlights militaries’ material interests, societal roles and socialties, and organizational divisions. In this article, I assess those factors for militaries in democracies while incorporating another consideration: civilian control and specifically the principle that militaries should obey the elected government’s orders. I argue that a crucial condition for defections in democracies is therefore executive self-coups. When protests are prompted by an executive’s attempts to decisively and illegally grab power, the military may see defecting as both necessary and justifiable. I find support for the importance of executive self-coups, combined with other conditions, using Qualitative Comparative Analysis of protests from 1991 to 2019 and case studies of Bolivia in 2019 and Ecuador in 2015.

articles.title: Relational Adaptation in Spot Trading
articles.abstract: Efficient adaptation to fluctuating market conditions is critical to economic agents’ survival and prosperity. Although theory highlights the value of relational contracts in facilitating adaptation, empirical evidence remains limited. Using wholesale transaction data, we show that a buyer initially sourcing on the spot market may repeatedly trade with a seller, offering a price premium in exchange for a relational contract that assures supply. The relational premium adjusts strategically to market-level supply shocks in a manner consistent with maximising the joint payoffs for the pair of traders. This efficient adaptation ensures the sustainability of relationships despite varying market demand and supply.

articles.title: Gambling for Re-election
articles.authors: Alastair Langtry, Niklas Potrafke, Marcel Schlepper, Timo Wochner
articles.abstract: We show that gambling-style behaviour is important in politics: politicians ‛gamble for re-election‚ in the context of a political leader selection. We exploit unique access to leaked information on MPs' individual decisions in the 2021 leadership election of Germany's centre-right parties. MPs are more likely to vote for a riskier candidate when facing lower re-election chances. These results match the predictions derived from our model of rational risk-taking. Gambling for re-election shows that MPs trade off leaders' expected quality against their riskiness. It provides a new explanation for intra-party dissent, and rationalises why parties may choose low quality leaders.

articles.title: Massive Open Online Courses and Labor Market Outcomes: Evidence from Colombia
articles.abstract: This paper studies the impact of MOOC certificates on labor market outcomes using a Coursera initiative that offered free certificates during the COVID-19 pandemic. Although eligibility for free certificates was randomized, course completion rates were low-only 6.2% of eligible participants completed at least one course-so we rely on an event-study design to estimate the effects of receiving a certificate. The results show that MOOC certificates increases formal employment by about 5 percentage points, with larger impacts among participants who were not employed at baseline and those from low-income households, and no clear differences by gender. These gains are concentrated in employment at larger firms and in economic sectors aligned with the course content. Overall, while MOOCs have the potential to improve employment outcomes, additional interventions appear necessary to increase course completion rates.

articles.title: Heterogeneous patience, population growth, and wealth accumulation
articles.abstract: We study a neoclassical growth model with population growth and heterogeneous agents. The model can be interpreted as either a Ramsey model with heterogeneous discounting and entry of new agents with zero endowments or an OLG model with infinitely-lived agents with different discount factors. We prove that, in the unique stationary equilibrium, agents other than the most patient may hold capital. Introducing public debt, a labor income tax, or a capital subsidy allows more agent types to save, reducing inequality among agents with different discount factors while increasing inequality among agents with the same discount factor entered in different periods.

articles.title: Seniority Amidst Change: Parliamentary Turnover and Persistence in 14 European Democracies
articles.abstract: This article provides a multi-dimensional perspective on parliamentary composition in an era of political turbulence. It extends existing turnover models by proposing a three-dimensional framework to understand persistence which includes the structure of the ballot, electoral volatility and institutional career opportunities. Using novel comparative data from 14 European democracies (1965–2021), where we distinguish between newcomers, seniors (3+ terms) and super-seniors (5+ terms), we find that persistence is most likely in politico-institutional contexts characterised by candidate control over ballot access, low electoral volatility and unicameral legislatures. Super-seniors seem to occupy an advantaged position, as prior seniority levels strongly shape subsequent ones, and they are also less vulnerable to electoral shocks. At the same time, we descriptively show that none of the countries in our sample provide the full configuration conducive to persistence, suggesting that contemporary democracies contain institutional arrangements that promote circulation within the legislative elite and limit concentration.

articles.title: Supporting Without Steering: The Role of International Actors in Colombia's Policy on Venezuelan Displacement
articles.abstract: Research on the role of international organisations (IOs) and donors in migration governance has largely focused on low‐income countries, while Latin America remains underrepresented despite the importance of its middle‐income states in responding to large‐scale displacement. This article examines Colombia's Temporary Protection Statute for Venezuelan Migrants (TPS), introduced in 2021 to grant Venezuelan nationals legal status, rights, and a pathway to permanent residency. Drawing on 65 interviews with policymakers and representatives of IOs and aid agencies, as well as policy documents, it analyses how Colombian authorities, IOs, and donors jointly shaped the policy. The findings show that international actors contributed through financial assistance, ideational framing, knowledge provision, and capacity‐building. Yet Colombian authorities retained policy ownership, selectively adapting and mobilising international resources to advance domestically defined objectives. The article demonstrates how extensive international involvement and domestic ownership can coexist, challenging portrayals of Southern states as reactive to external agendas.

articles.title: From Taiwan Dream to Everyday Resilience: Temporal Trajectories of Vietnamese Marriage Migrant Women in Taiwan
articles.authors: Huynh Le Anh Huy, Huynh Quoc Tuan
articles.abstract: Marriage migration from Vietnam to Taiwan has often been portrayed in static terms of integration or failure, overlooking how women adapt to ruptures across time. This study applies resilience theory to examine how 27 Vietnamese marriage migrant women confronted disappointment and developed coping strategies within transnational marriages. Drawing on in‐depth interviews, the findings reveal that Vietnamese marriage migrant women endured disillusionments such as domestic violence, neglect, and isolation but actively recalibrated their lives through spirituality practices, small‐scale entrepreneurship and investments in children's education. By situating these practices within a resilience framework, the study highlights how adaptation is not a linear recovery but an iterative process shaped by agency, family obligations and cross‐border ties. Through this perspective, the study shows how aspiration, rupture and recalibration recur across the life course, leading to different rather than converging trajectories. The study extends resilience theory into the domain of marriage migration, contributes to feminist and transnational scholarship by foregrounding everyday agency, and carries policy implications for supporting migrant women beyond early settlement stages.

articles.title: Migration and Education Choices: How Low‐Skilled Migration Shapes the Educational Attainment of Mexican Youth
articles.abstract: This paper examines the impact of low‐skilled migration on educational attainment in developing countries, specifically focusing on Mexico. While previous research has extensively studied brain drain (the migration of high‐skilled workers to developed countries), this study delves into the lesser‐discussed phenomenon of ‘brawn drain’, which involves the migration of low‐skilled workers to developed nations. The paper analyses data from the Mesoamerican Migration Project to understand how the presence of low‐skilled migrant elders (household members aged 26 or older) affects the educational decisions of young individuals (ages 18–25) in high‐migration communities. The results reveal a strong negative impact of family‐level exposure to low‐skilled US migrants on Mexican youth, discouraging them from pursuing further education. The study explores other factors, such as community‐level influences and the presence of high‐skilled individuals as role models, on educational outcomes. Overall, the paper contributes valuable insights to the understanding of how low‐skilled migration affects educational attainment in developing countries like Mexico.

articles.title: Unrest, Shifting Power, and Death-Watch War
articles.abstract: Domestic unrest often creates problems of both shifting power and shifting preferences. We analyze a model in which a foreign state considers a “death-watch” attack against a domestic state temporarily weakened by unrest in which (1) two polarized factions compete for the power to set policy in the future and (2) the foreign state’s favored faction may support an invasion. Military success allows the foreign state to seize policy control, but defeat may hasten the rise of its disfavored faction when the favored faction links the outcomes of the two conflicts by bandwagoning with the attacker. In equilibrium, decisions to attack and bandwagon depend on the interaction of shifting power and shifting preferences. We show first that temporary weakness causes war, but only when the favored faction is unlikely to survive unrest. Second, increasing factional polarization can encourage or discourage foreign attack and local bandwagoning, conditional on how domestic preferences are shifting. Third, extensions show that (1) death-watch attacks are possible at any distribution of power; (2) the threat of attack may not be sufficient to deter domestic unrest; and (3) attack may be profitable even when alternative options of aiding a favored faction are available. We also use the model to explain why similar episodes of unrest in Ukraine prompted Russian invasion in 2014 but not 2004.

articles.title: Contestation of International Organizations: Patterns, Drivers, and Responses
articles.authors: Jonas Tallberg, Stefanie Walter, Michael Zürn
articles.abstract: The contestation of international organizations (IOs) over past decades has inspired a rich research program. This essay takes stock of progress by reviewing key findings in existing scholarship and identifying critical areas for future study. We propose a typology that distinguishes between internal contestation, which criticizes the institutions or policies of an IO with the aim of reform, and external contestation, which challenges an IO’s foundational principles and very existence. Building on this conceptual distinction, we review the most important findings of existing research on three key themes: patterns of contestation, drivers of contestation, and responses to contestation. We also argue that this conceptualization helps us better understand the changing nature of contestation: while criticism of how IOs function has long been a staple of world politics, it recently appears to have shifted toward a deeper form involving more fundamental questioning of IOs themselves. We conclude by highlighting the need for dynamic theories and improved measurements to explain when and how IO contestation shifts from internal criticism to external rejection, and by outlining a forward-looking research agenda on organizational robustness, hegemonic contestation, and the relationship between IO contestation and the broader contestation of global governance.

articles.title: Ideology, revolutionary redistribution, and mobilization in civil war
articles.abstract: Armed groups frequently intervene in civilian life during civil war, but the consequences of such interventions for their military mobilization remain poorly understood. We argue that revolutionary social intervention, when driven by a radical ideology, induces a trade-off for armed groups in military mobilization. While radical social intervention effectively mobilizes ideologically congruent supporters, it imposes significant costs on the broader population and discourages their participation in the revolutionary army. We illustrate this argument with evidence from the Chinese Civil War (1946–1949), focusing on how revolutionary land reform by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) affected its wartime military mobilization. Leveraging a novel dataset on about 220,000 martyred CCP soldiers, we estimate how land reform affected the CCP’s recruitment of soldiers and their battle death rates with a difference-in-differences design. We find a substantial decrease in the CCP’s recruitment of new soldiers after land reform, consistent with historical accounts emphasizing the campaign’s extensive victimization of civilians. Additionally, we find that soldiers who enlisted after land reform died at significantly higher rates, suggesting that the campaign drew more ideologically committed recruits with greater combat motivation into the CCP’s army. Our findings shed new light on how ideology shapes mobilization outcomes in civil war.

Children from six cultures reliably help their peers—but in different ways
articles.authors: Henriette Zeidler, Marie Schäfer, Esther Herrmann, Patricia Kanngiesser, Luke Maurits, Daniel Haun, Michael Tomasello
articles.abstract: Helping others is an integral part of human sociality, but systematic cross-cultural comparisons of children’s helping behavior are rare. Existing work has mainly focused on interactions between adults and children, paying less attention to peer dynamics—which are more relevant in many cultural settings. Here, we report a study of 4- to 9-y-old children’s (N = 336) spontaneous helping in 6 highly diverse populations in Latin America, Africa, and Europe (Wichí, Quechua, ≠Akhoe Hai||om, Samburu, Kikuyu, and Germans). In all settings, we observed pairs of same-aged children in an experimental task in which one partner could assist the other by providing either instrumental help or information. Across cultures, children reliably helped their peers by offering either type of help, with the provision of information increasing over age. We found striking commonalities in peer helping in all settings, with only small culture-specific patterns in children’s responses. This suggests that helping among children is a universal human behavior which is subtly shaped by local norms and practices.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence and Punctuated Equilibrium: Shaping Government Attention in the Digital Age
articles.authors: Shuo Chen, Yiran Li, Yuzheng Wang
articles.abstract: How do government attention and policy agendas shift when information constraints are relaxed through technological advancement? Punctuated equilibrium theory links agenda‐setting dynamics to governments' limited information‐processing capabilities, yet we know little about whether and how technology improvement such as artificial intelligence (AI) influences policy agendas. This article proposes a conditional digital punctuation framework to specify the conditions under which technological advancements drive agenda shifts. Using China's implementation of AI initiatives as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that government attention exhibits a punctuated pattern. AI increases technology‐focused attention, signaling incremental changes, while having minimal impact on general government attention. This selective impact stems from AI's asymmetric effects on information processing. Specifically, AI significantly increases the procurement‐based indicator of information quantity, which is associated with greater attention to technology sectors; however, no significant change is observed in the corresponding indicator of information quality, consistent with its limited impact on general government attention.

articles.title: Hindered From Making a Difference: How Increasing Organizational Constraints Undermine Public Servants' Perceptions of Prosocial Impact and Why It Matters
articles.abstract: Public servants often work under organizational constraints that hinder how they experience and carry out their work. Drawing on conservation of resources theory, this research examines how changes in these constraints affect public servants' perceptions that their work benefits others and, in turn, their well‐being and withdrawal behavior. Using data from two longitudinal studies conducted in the United States and France, the findings show that increases in organizational constraints are associated with declines in perceived prosocial impact, which in turn predict lower well‐being and greater withdrawal over time. These results identify perceived prosocial impact as a key psychological resource that links changing work conditions to employee functioning. By emphasizing the dynamic nature of organizational constraints, this study advances the understanding of how evolving administrative conditions can weaken the psychological foundations that sustain meaningful and effective public service.

articles.title: A Response to Don Kettl's Debate Article on the Future of Public Administration and Democracy
articles.abstract: This commentary critically engages with Kettl's analysis of the crisis of public administration (PA) scholarship and its relationship with democratic decline. It argues that both phenomena should be understood within broader global developments rather than primarily as problems specific to the United States. While acknowledging the role of governance failures in facilitating autocratization, it questions the claim that autocratization results predominantly from the failures of PA scholarship and practice. Rather, it emphasizes that broader societal phenomena, such as the erosion of societal trust and the power‐consolidating objectives of authoritarian leaders play a key role. Drawing on Hungary's experience, the commentary illustrates how authoritarian governance may perpetuate administrative instability and institutional transformation long after the (perceived) failures of democratic governance have been addressed in the early phase of illiberal transformation. However, it also argues that poor governance and declining policy performance can eventually undermine authoritarian rule, as illustrated by Hungary's 2026 political transformation. The commentary thus highlights the complex and potentially self‐undermining relationship between authoritarianism and public governance.

articles.title: Is Public Sector a Better Place for Moms to Work? Exploring Sector Difference in Child Penalties on Women
articles.abstract: With commonly stabler and more flexible working environment, is public sector a better place for moms to work? Theorizing child penalties from sector difference perspective, we argue that childbirth may cause less gender gaps in unemployment and earnings but greater gender disparities in working time commitments in the public sector since job stability and family‐friendliness may form gender norms that depreciate women's work in the public sector. We test our hypotheses by employing event study designs using data from China Family Panel Studies (2010–2022). We found that women public employees experienced smaller child penalties in unemployment and earnings while greater child penalties in working hours than private counterparts, which can be explained by greater family responsibilities and spousal depreciation of women's jobs after childbirth. This paper advances theories of gender equity in public administration by proposing distinct child penalties in the public sector that challenges conventional beliefs.

articles.title: A Public Philosophy for Public Administration in Times of Democratic Crisis
articles.abstract: Public administration is at the center of the global democratic crisis. Meeting this challenge requires more than managerial and analytic competence—it requires a public philosophy grounded in the first principles of democratic ethos. We offer such a philosophy, drawing on four seminal thinkers whose concepts reflect the conditions public administrators face in times of democratic crisis. Judith Shklar's liberalism of fear establishes a negative obligation to refuse cruelty and resist its institutionalization. Alasdair MacIntyre's internal goods of practice create a positive obligation to cultivate virtue and protect the integrity of administrative practice. Isaiah Berlin's agony of choice obligates administrators to acknowledge irreducible value conflicts and their consequential impact on democratic life. Hannah Arendt's enlarged mentality provides a framework for thinking across perspectives so that judgment under conflict becomes democratically defensible. Together, these concepts form a public philosophy for public administration with practical significance for administrative judgment, organizational culture, and institutional courage.

articles.title: The Marginal Propensity to Hire
articles.abstract: When financial constraints bind, firms adjust employment in response to cash flow shocks. A 2010 revaluation of business rates, a UK tax levied on business-occupied properties, implied that similar firms, occupying similar properties in narrow geographical locations, experienced different tax changes. I find that, on average, for every ￡1 of additional cash flow triggered by the tax change, 39 pence were spent on employment, with small and leveraged firms responding the most. I use these findings to discipline a general equilibrium model with firm heterogeneity and financial frictions and quantitatively determine the aggregate effects of a fiscal transfer to firms.

articles.title: Are Markups Too High? Competition, Strategic Innovation, and Industry Dynamics
articles.authors: Laurent Cavenaile, Murat Alp Celik, Xu Tian
articles.abstract: To study competition, innovation, and industry dynamics that arise as a result of their interaction, we develop a new oligopolistic general-equilibrium Schumpeterian growth model. This model ties together the endogenous growth, oligopolistic competition, and dynamic industrial organization literatures in a single unified framework. Within each industry, there are an endogenously determined number of large firms (“superstars”) that compete á la Cournot and a continuum of small firms which collectively constitute a competitive fringe. Firms dynamically choose their innovation strategies, cognizant of other firms' choices, and their entry and exit are endogenous. The model is consistent with the macroeconomic trends observed in the United States since the 1970s, such as the domination of industries by a small number of superstar firms, the rise of markups, market concentration, profits, and R&D spending, and the decline in business dynamism, productivity growth, and the labor share. It replicates the empirical relationship between innovation and competition within and across industries. As an application, we estimate the model to disentangle the effects of separate mechanisms on the structural transition observed in the United States, which yields striking results: (1) While the increase in the average markup causes a significant static welfare loss, this loss is overshadowed by the dynamic welfare gains from increased innovation in response to higher profit opportunities. (2) The increasing costs of innovation are found to be the primary determinant of lackluster productivity growth, i.e., ideas are getting harder to find.

articles.title: Data everywhere, but are they fit for purpose?
articles.abstract: Vast amounts of new data are fundamentally shaping how people manage their lives and do their work. The volume is overwhelming—Google Dataset Search discovers 2 million new datasets every month—and so are the uses by scientists, governments, and the public. Governments across the world are treating data as a strategic asset. But data alone are not enough. Infrastructure must be developed that can provide signals about which data are “fit for purpose” for the increasingly vast number of potential uses. Informed and appropriate use is, after all, the ultimate objective of making data available for the public good.

Populism as a problem of social segregation: socioeconomic composition of personal networks and populist voting
articles.authors: Bernardo Mackenna, Ricardo González, Adolfo Fuentes, Esteban Muñoz
articles.abstract: Responding to recent calls to understand populism as a problem of social integration, this article proposes a network segregation perspective for the study of populism. Specifically, it theorizes that populist voting is shaped by the socioeconomic composition of individuals’ personal networks. Combining cross-national survey data from approximately 18,000 respondents in 19 countries with expert surveys on parties’ populism, empirical analyses suggest that the socioeconomic status of personal network contacts is strongly and robustly associated with populist voting. Across multiple estimators, model specifications, and definitions of populism, we show that while the socioeconomic diversity of personal networks appears unrelated to populist voting, those with ties to higher-status individuals are consistently less likely to vote for populist candidates. Additional analysis shows that the latter association is stronger among higher-status individuals, consistent with an interpretation in which individual and network status are mutually reinforcing. These findings highlight how personal networks can help specify the mechanisms linking socioeconomic processes with populist politics.

articles.title: Teaching the past, informing the present? School history education and attitudes toward foreign countries
articles.abstract: How does school history education emphasizing past grievances with other countries impact attitudes toward conflict and cooperation with the countries today? We examine this question using original data from 34 classrooms across 17 high schools in Seoul, South Korea. We first test whether exposure to anti‐Japanese content in school history education negatively impacts students' attitudes toward cooperation with Japan. We then compare how the attitudes of students educated with a more pro‐US textbook differ from those using a more anti‐US one. We find that school history education influenced what historical events students believed as “facts” and their evaluation of historical events. However, the effect on students' historical memories did not by itself automatically translate into corresponding attitudes toward present‐day Japan or the United States. Our findings offer various implications for studies on international rivalries and historical memories, as well as for debates on the political effects of school education.

articles.title: A Suitable Groom: The Effect of Girl's Education on Dowry Payments
articles.abstract: The social and economic costs of marriage for the bride represent a significant burden for low‐/middle‐income families, contributing to the disempowerment of women within their natal and marital households in multiple ways. This paper uses a large‐scale primary dataset from rural eastern India to investigate the association of dowry with women's education. We test two hypotheses: (a) the human capital effect, that is, the reduction in dowry because of an increase in the acquisition of human capital thereby improving her economic circumstances; (b) the hypergamy effect, that is, education can increase the incidence of dowry via the search for a potentially higher‐education attaining groom who will demand a higher dowry payment in the “marriage market.” Since the level of education of the women may itself be affected by dowry concerns and so is potentially endogenous, we use a state educational developmental policy as an intervention to understand the variegated impact of higher education attainment by women. Finally, the analysis shows an overall effect of the educational status of young women on the dowry payments made by their families, accounting for their distinction across two characteristics, higher human capital acquisition and greater potential to match a more educated groom in the marriage market.

articles.title: Same‐Sex Marriage in Times of Political Uncertainty: Evidence from Brazil
articles.authors: Fernanda de Fortes de Lena, Samuel Araujo Gomes da Silva, Enrique Acosta
articles.abstract: This research note examines how political polarization and the fragility of same‐sex marriage rights in Brazil shaped marriage patterns over the past decade. Using civil registry data from 2013 to 2023, we focus on presidential election periods as moments of political uncertainty. The 2018 election of Jair Bolsonaro, whose campaign was marked by anti‐LGBTQ+ rhetoric, coincided with a nationwide surge in same‐sex marriages: female couples registered increases of approximately 94 percent and male couples approximately 71 percent above expected levels, while different‐sex marriages remained stable. No comparable surge occurred in the 2022 election, suggesting that the novelty and perceived credibility of the threat drove the 2018 increase. Results further reveal gendered dynamics in mean age at marriage (MAM): among female same‐sex couples, MAM reached its lowest point in 2018 across most regions, consistent with younger women anticipating family formation in response to the political threat, while no comparable shift is observed among male couples. Together, these findings suggest that same‐sex marriage in Brazil functions not only as an affective milestone but as a reactive act of legal protection—a dual character that points to the need for marriage theory to fully account for the drives of same‐sex marriage and its meanings.

articles.abstract: Previous research suggests that people who identify with global communities tend to show greater concern for global challenges. Using student samples from 44 countries across different cultural clusters ( N = 13,055), we examined whether (1) three forms of dispositional global social identification (GSI, with all humanity, citizens of the world, and people all over the world) are related to concern for global issues, (2) situational activation of these identifications increases such concern, (3) country‐level traditional and survival values are negatively associated with global concern, and (4) these values moderate the GSI–concern link. Both dispositional and situational GSIs positively predicted global concern. Situational activation showed inconsistent effects, whereas dispositional GSIs demonstrated moderate and consistent associations with global concern across the full sample and most countries. Overall, dispositional forms of GSI appeared more influential than situational ones. Contrary to expectations, traditional values (and survival values—marginally) were positively related to global concern and showed no evidence of moderating GSI–concern associations. Additional analyses showed the indices of GDP per capita, Human Development, Gini, and poverty as robust predictors of global concern. We discuss how these findings refine claims about the universality of global identification outcomes and highlight the importance of socio‐cultural context in shaping such concern.

articles.title: Bad news for (young) gamers: Using gaming platforms as news sources is more intimately associated with radical belief dispositions than other online spaces
articles.authors: Simon Greipl, Ulrike Schwertberger, Diana Rieger, Brigitte Naderer
articles.abstract: This study explores how digital news use among young Europeans links to radical belief dispositions, particularly within gaming platforms and messengers, where socio‐affective dynamics shape engagement with political information. We argue that online groups are an overlooked locus for biased information processing and the normalization of extremist worldviews. The conflation of an increasingly fragmented online news space with the inherently politicized gaming cosmos can relate to amplified problematic worldviews based on shared activity, identity, and reality. Based on a cross‐country survey ( N = 1489; eight European countries), we compare (the use of) gaming, messenger apps, social media, and traditional media for news in terms of how they afford problematic forms of collectivity, particularly in relation to social, cynical, and radical epistemologies. We find a robust correlation between news use and a set of radical belief dispositions, prominently with messenger apps, but even more so in gaming‐related online environments—less so on social media and none with traditional news use. Notably, a mediation analysis suggests that shared meaning‐making exhibits a negative rather than a positive indirect association with radical belief dispositions. We discuss the complex interplay of how individual factors and platform architectures connect with news engagement utilizing a vulnerability‐affordance framework.

articles.title: How perceived economic inequality shapes political efficacy: The mediating role of institutional trust
articles.authors: Mar Montoya‐Lozano, Guillermo B. Willis, Juan Diego García‐Castro, Rosa Rodríguez‐Bailón
articles.abstract: Economic inequality shapes citizens' attitudes and democratic support, yet little is known about how perceived inequality influences political efficacy. This research examines the relationship between perceived economic inequality and political efficacy, testing institutional trust as a psychosocial mechanism underlying this link. Across two correlational and two experimental studies, we present converging evidence for this process. Study 1 ( N = 9985) revealed multilevel evidence of a negative association between perceived economic inequality and institutional trust, beyond the effect of objective inequality, using Latin American survey data. Study 2 ( N = 1536) replicated this finding with a Spanish quota sample, revealing an indirect effect of perceived inequality on political efficacy through institutional trust. Study 3 ( N = 168) involved the experimental manipulation of inequality. Participants in the high‐inequality condition reported lower institutional trust and political efficacy, and the indirect effect was replicated. Study 4 ( N = 638) employed a concurrent double‐randomization design to manipulate perceived inequality and institutional trust. In contexts of high institutional trust, political efficacy differed between highly and less unequal conditions, with lower political efficacy observed in the high‐inequality condition. Similar patterns emerged for collective action. Overall, perceived inequality undermines institutional trust, reducing political efficacy and democratic engagement.

articles.title: Conceptualizing and measuring global consciousness
articles.authors: James H. Liu, Robert Jiqi Zhang, Jacky C. K. Ng, Sylvia Xiaohua Chen
articles.abstract: To examine the conceptualization and the measurement of global consciousness (GC) in cross‐national contexts, we conducted a secondary analysis on survey data collected from 16,241 individuals across 35 societies. Results demonstrate that GC is best conceptualized as a multidimensional construct by a bifactor ESEM model, in which GC captures an overarching and direct source of common variance across all manifest indicators, whereas domain‐specific residual variance is retained by three existing measures: Identification with All Humanity (IWAH), Cosmopolitan Orientation (COS), and a shortened version of Global Orientations (GOS). Metric invariance was successfully achieved across 30 out of 35 societies. At the individual level, GC was negatively associated with political conservatism, an effect that was amplified in societies with higher HDI, more robust rule of law, and a salient culture of individualism. In an exploratory societal‐level analysis, aggregated GC functioned as an informative ecological indicator, appearing more prominent in the Global South societies across the sample. This preliminary pattern is probably attributable to the open system where GC is measured, reflecting the hopes and aspirations of people in the making.

articles.title: Making Policy Evidence Traceable: A Modular Preregistration Framework for Policy Evaluation
articles.authors: Yiyun Xia, Tianhao Zhao, Yuhao Ba
articles.abstract: Preregistration is increasingly used in policy research, but its value depends on whether preregistered commitments can be clearly linked to reported analyses. Policy studies often involve multiple outcomes, evolving administrative data, consequential design and analytic choices, and adaptive implementation, making it difficult to distinguish prespecified tests from subsequent adjustments. This research note proposes a modular, policy‐oriented companion framework for using existing preregistration infrastructure. The framework combines a shared core that defines the estimand, outcomes, and identification strategy with design‐specific modules for field experiments, administrative‐data quasi‐experiments, and behavioral policy trials. Together, the components serve two purposes: claim traceability, by linking reported results to the original plan, and governed adaptation, by providing a transparent record of changes made during the study. The aim is not to prevent adaptation, but to show which analyses were prespecified, which were revised through documented amendments, and which were developed later. This approach aims to improve the interpretability and transparency of policy research while remaining feasible in applied policy settings.

articles.title: Questionnaire Democrats? Reconsidering the Relevance of Abstract Democracy Support in the American Public
articles.abstract: The American public largely favors “democracy,” yet many citizens tolerate undemocratic actions and candidates. This raises doubts about the relevance of abstract democracy support to actual democratic commitment. In contrast, we argue that abstract democracy support is a normatively significant dimension of attitude variation among Americans. Using nineteen surveys fielded between 1995 and 2024, we show that a sizable segment of the public expresses only tepid support for democracy, and that a nontrivial minority expresses opposition. Moreover, commonly used abstract democracy support items converge on a single latent construct which displays high rank-order stability, but also meaningful within-person variation, over a two-year period. Abstract democracy support negatively predicts openness to a wide range of electoral and liberal democratic violations and is associated with greater likelihood of electorally punishing anti-democratic candidates. In panel data, positive within-person deviations in abstract democracy support precede negative within-person deviations in openness to authoritarian governance, suggesting that individual-level shifts in abstract support predict later change in substantive democracy attitudes. Overall our findings suggest that the value of ‘democracy’ is contested among Americans, with potential implications for democratic erosion. We recommend that efforts to understand the American public’s role in democratic backsliding and restoration treat abstract support as a distinct attitude construct, measure it with multi-item scales, and explore whether or not it possesses causal significance.

articles.title: How Policy Design Affects Perceptions of Beneficiaries and Support for Welfare
articles.abstract: Most of the public supports welfare policies in the abstract, but many hold deep misgivings about the deservingness of welfare recipients, driving down support for specific policies. Welfare policies are often designed to mitigate these concerns by restricting access to benefits, but it is unclear to what effect. According to an influential strain of research drawing on social construction theory, these restrictions may backfire, instead increasing concerns about a free-riding public. In contrast -- drawing on psychological research on the deservingness heuristic -- I argue that policy features, such as work requirements, signal effort on behalf of recipients and thus deservingness. Using an experiment, I find that several policy features increase perceptions of deservingness and, in turn, increase policy support and generosity. However, some policy features are also perceived as overly burdensome, reducing the effects on policy support. Treatment effects on perceptions of beneficiary deservingness are largest among ambivalent respondents, but largely generalize across partisanship, ideology, and racial resentment. Overall, these findings help clarify the implications of the deservingness heuristic while challenging predictions from social construction theory and informing ongoing debates over public opinion and policy feedback.

articles.title: Decoding Corruption Cycles: Extractive versus Collusive Corruption
What Works Against Populist Rhetoric? The Effects of Counter-Arguments on Democratic Attitudes
articles.abstract: Politicians use populist rhetoric – arguments that portray politics as an enduring conflict between “the good people” and “the evil elites” – to generate support for attacks on constitutional safeguards, the media, and minorities. Yet, little is known about how to counteract such rhetoric. We utilize a pre-registered survey experiment in the UK (n $$\cong$$ 4000) to investigate the effects of counter-arguments put forward by fellow citizens. We hypothesize pluralist and democratic elitist counter-arguments to be promising antidotes to populist rhetoric and test to what extent such arguments can strengthen liberal democratic attitudes and weaken populist majoritarian ones. We find that populism can be challenged successfully but not with all types of counter-arguments. Pluralist appeals can decrease support for populist majoritarian democracy, while elitist counter-arguments have no effect on democratic attitudes. Additional analyses suggest that counter-arguments might also affect how voters evaluate candidates. These results contribute by demonstrating the potentials of counter-arguments in strengthening the resilience of liberal democracies vis-à-vis populist challenges.

articles.title: O Xenos: Racial Difference, Colorism, and Attitudes Toward Immigrants in Greece
Democratic but Still White: The Impact of Racial Identity Threats on White Democrats’ Support for Racial Justice Protests
articles.abstract: In recent years, observers have noted an apparent increase in racially progressive attitudes among White Democrats. Among journalists, this “great awokening” of White Democrats is practically taken as a political fact. However, what this consensus about the racial liberalism of White Democrats often overlooks is that while White Democrats have in many ways moved in line with the Democratic Party’s position on race and racial inequality, their White identity makes them vulnerable to racial identity threats. In this study, I test this potential for racial identity-driven backlash among White Democrats in the context of racial justice protest movements. To do this, I conduct a survey experiment in which respondents are exposed to an image from a racial justice protest, and I vary the messaging on the signs in the image as well as the race of the protesters. I find that when protesters use messaging that is critical of Whites and Whiteness, White Democrats’ support for the movement and the protesters declines. Additionally, such messaging causes respondents to distance themselves from the views of the protesters and raises concerns about violence erupting at the protests. These results underscore how racial identity threats can erode White Democrats’ support for political messages and political movements that their increasingly liberal racial attitudes should make them amenable to.

articles.title: Un-Priming Politics: A Method to Reduce Overreporting of Political Engagement
articles.authors: Elizabeth C. Connors, John V. Kane
articles.abstract: Survey researchers frequently employ measures of political engagement, yet social desirability pressures can lead to overreporting. Building upon existing literature, we adopt an iterative approach to determine how such overreporting can be reduced. Four preregistered survey experiments were conducted (total N=7,122). We first confirm that social desirability considerations can underlie some types of self-reported political engagement. Second, having tested a variety of interventions that were designed to reduce overreporting, we find that our most effective treatment ( Dampen Politics) was one that aimed to decrease the salience of politics. This treatment significantly reduced (1) the degree to which respondents perceived the survey as political, and (2) some types of self-reported political engagement, particularly political interest and voting. We tested alternative implementations of the Dampen Politics treatment, each time assessing its robustness and validity. Our findings suggest a simple adjustment in survey wording and organization can meaningfully decrease overreporting of political engagement.

articles.title: The Role of Sex Ratios in Refugee Inflows and Gendered Host Attitudes: A Vignette Survey Experiment in a German State
articles.authors: Chia-Jung Tsai, Robert G. Rinderknecht, John R.B. Palmer, Emilio Zagheni
articles.abstract: This study investigates how the sex ratio of refugee populations can shape attitudes toward refugee inflows in a German state. We use an online vignette survey experiment to examine respondents’ nonacceptance of refugee arrivals and four types of perceived threats: job competition, mate competition, threats to German culture, and safety. Respondents are recruited via Meta targeted online advertisement in the German state of Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania. Our results suggest that nonacceptance of a refugee group increases as its male-to-female sex ratio rises. This relationship is particularly pronounced for perceived threats to German culture and safety, when the refugee group is non-white. Respondents’ gender also shapes both overall acceptance and the specific threats that respondents perceive. Female respondents showed more tolerant attitudes than male respondents toward refugee groups with lower male-to-female sex ratios. Female respondents also perceived greater threats to culture and mate competition in the neighborhood from non-white male refugees. Male respondents perceived greater threats from job competition. Both groups showed heightened perceived threats to safety. Overall, our findings show that the demographic composition of refugee inflows interacts with respondent gender to produce distinct patterns of acceptance and threat perception, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying negative attitudes toward refugee arrivals in Germany.

articles.title: The Circuitous Routes to Permanence: Understanding International Students’ Permit Transition Pathways to Permanent Residency in Canada
articles.authors: Jonathan Anim Amoyaw, Yoko Yoshida, Michael Haan, George Botchey
articles.abstract: As countries adopt a “two-step” immigrant selection process, understanding how temporary residents granted study or work permit(s) transition to permanent residency (PR) is crucial. Using linked administrative records and sequence and cluster analysis, we identify five permit transition pathways to PR among international students that vary by timing, duration, and permit sequence. Our multinomial logistic regression analysis highlights pathway differences across study level, arrival cohort, and province. Students pursuing a master's degree or non-university diploma were more likely to obtain off-campus work permit(s) during studies and a post-study work permit before PR. Post-2008 cohorts were also more likely to follow this pathway. Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and Quebec stood out for transitions to PR without a post-study work permit. This study reveals complex, non-linear transitions to PR, emphasizing the role of evolving immigration policies in shaping diverse pathways. Insights can inform discussions on temporary status transitions and differential access to PR.

articles.title: Romania’s immigration debate under neoliberal hegemony: Constructing diligent migrants and individualising Transylvanian Hungarians as racist
articles.abstract: In 2020, a group of residents of the rural Transylvanian Hungarian-majority municipality of Ditró (in Hungarian), or Ditrău (in Romanian), mobilised themselves against two Sri Lankan bakers. Mainstream media portrayed the incident as xenophobic and racist, the locals as right-wing extremists, and the Sri Lankans as merely ‘migrant workers’, turning the ‘Ditrău incident’ into Romania’s first and most important nationwide immigration debate. This article analyses what the media-coverage of these events tells us about the country’s approach to immigration, and how the symbols, signs, languages, meanings, knowledges, and memories articulated around the ‘Ditrău incident’ make this and other relatable events feed into this approach. We employ discourse analysis, including Lotman’s cultural semiotics, and engage with the institutional, political, and historical framing of ‘the incident’, as well as the broader socio-political and historical context of Romania’s immigration debate. In this way, we argue that, first, the ‘Ditrău incident’ was instrumental to Romania’s dominant societal core in portraying itself as closer to ‘the West’, its absolution of any responsibility for xenophobia and racism, the reproduction of the hegemony of neoliberalism and the middle-class ideology, and the construction of ‘diligent migrant workers’. Second, ‘the incident’ was fundamental in the silencing, individualisation, and invisibilisation of working-class voices and particularising Transylvanian Hungarians as racists and extremists. Finally, it allowed Romanian mainstream actors to brand their nation as open, tolerant, and humane, while normalising the commodification and overexploitation of third-country migrant labour.

articles.title: Powered by (discrete) emotions? The consequences of affective polarization for self-censorship and outgroup silencing
articles.authors: Luna Laufer, Laura Gerstner, Pia Kinzler, Julia Stockwald, Anna-Luisa Sacher, Carsten Reinemann
articles.abstract: Amid ongoing debates about political polarization in Western Democracies, this study investigates the role of affective polarization in the context of practices related to political discourse. In doing so, it moves beyond generalized affective polarization and delves into discrete negative emotions (fear, disgust, and anger), examining how they relate to the willingness to engage in self-censorship and the belief in the importance of silencing others, i.e., the respective political outgroup. Findings from a quota-based online survey conducted in autumn 2024 in Germany ( N = 1,918) reveal that the effects of affective polarization vary depending on the underlying emotion: fear of the political outgroup is linked to an increased willingness to self-censor. In contrast, anger is associated with a reduced willingness to self-censor, while all three negative emotions are connected to a higher belief in the importance to silence the political outgroup. These results underscore the critical role of discrete emotions in affective polarization, offering nuanced insights that extend beyond generalized dislike. In addition, they provide valuable insights into how affective polarization may threaten democratic values.

articles.title: Debate and Legislative Productivity in US State Legislatures
articles.abstract: Scholarship holds that procedural rules shape legislative proceedings, but most existing evidence comes from the US Congress' limited procedural variation. This article develops a theoretical framework for how different forms of debate restriction—both limits on member participation and procedural hurdles to closing debate—affect legislative productivity, and how these effects depend on chambers' institutional capacity. Using an original dataset of debate rules and bill progression spanning 2011–2018 from all 99 US state legislative chambers, we show that restrictions on member speaking opportunities and ending debate are associated with higher legislative productivity, with the relationship operating through distinct mechanisms. Procedural hurdles to ending debate are associated with higher productivity in low‐professionalism legislatures, while these associations diminish or reverse in more professionalized chambers. These findings demonstrate the conditional nature of debate rules and institutional capacity, offering new insight into procedural designs and the tradeoff between deliberation and efficiency in lawmaking.

articles.title: Party and Prejudice: Are Asian American Candidates Better Suited to Win in White Districts?
articles.authors: Eric Gonzalez Juenke, Paru Shah, Bernard L. Fraga
articles.abstract: Recent work on Asian American descriptive representation has found that Asian American officeholders are more prevalent in racially diverse districts when compared to Black or Latino representatives, but still face substantial obstacles in very white electoral districts. This work, however, models Asian American representation by observing officeholders only, ignoring both the competitive election environment and Asian American losing candidates, biasing its inferences. We reassess these conclusions using a candidate‐centered approach in thousands of state legislative races in 2018 and 2020. Our results demonstrate that Asian American, Black, and Latino candidates all perform substantially better in white districts than officeholder models predict, and that any differences between minority groups in white districts are due to the partisan match between candidates and their districts. The findings speak to the need for researchers to model vote choice as a candidate‐centered process, paying careful attention to the actual choices on voters' election day ballots.

Wait for It: Why Authoritarians Reshuffle Ruling Coalitions After Elections
articles.abstract: This article asks whether elections, even if they are not free and fair, might still have important consequences for authoritarian ruling coalitions, testing the theory that dictators avoid destabilizing their coalition before an election, but can afford to do this once the vote has passed. Disregarding the competitiveness and integrity of elections, the post-electoral period may serve as a face-saving time for resignations and as an opportunity for promotions or other cabinet changes, which autocrats can leverage to manage elites. Examining panel data on authoritarian regimes that held presidential elections in which the incumbent retained office between 1967 and 2023, I find that cabinet turnover is significantly higher in the period following elections. By exploiting the quasi-exogenous timing of scheduled elections and multiple robustness checks, the analysis shows that elections trigger elite reshuffling rather than merely coinciding with it.

articles.title: The sequential replicant effect in interpersonal sincerity: evidence from AI-mediated apology and gratitude
articles.abstract: Sincerity, a core interpersonal value that mobilizes emotional resources, faces distinct challenges in AI-mediated interpersonal contexts. Extending the Replicant Effect from informational trust to interpersonal sincerity, this study examines how AIMC awareness and AI involvement cues shape sincerity judgments and subsequent relational responses. Drawing on two pre-registered, two-round studies in apology (N = 546) and gratitude (N = 561) scenarios, we found that AI involvement cues reliably reduced perceived sincerity. Primed AIMC awareness showed a more sequential influence on later no-cue evaluations through AIMC suspicion. High-ambiguity AI cues produced sequential effects only in the gratitude context. These findings suggest that hybrid human-AI authorship may reshape how interpersonal sincerity is inferred and validated, while also showing that the effects of AI cues and AIMC awareness depend on cue clarity and relational context.

The relationship between EU fiscal transfers and the European policy profile of political parties
articles.abstract: This research note examines how fiscal transfers within the European Union shape the programmatic strategies of domestic political parties. We argue that a country’s net-contributor or net-receiving status conditions the strategies how parties articulate their positions on European integration. In net-receiving states, Euroskeptic parties strategically mute EU-related rhetoric to avoid undermining their broader policy stance. Moreover, the increase in pro-EU positions among parties in net-receiving states is driven mainly by support for further EU-level redistribution. We evaluate these claims using Chapel Hill Expert Survey data from 2002–2024 and a regression discontinuity design that uses continuous measures of net contributions to the EU budget. The empirical analyses, in which we also test for a linear relationship, align with our expectations. Euroskeptic parties mention the EU less in net-receiving contexts while beneficiary status solely shifts party positions toward pro-redistribution preferences at the EU level. These results illustrate how Euroskeptic parties cope with the potential positive impacts of the EU.
