articles.title: The inequality of voice: how belonging to lower social status groups impacts worker voice
articles.authors: Arjuna Snoep-Delleman, Agnes Akkerman, Katerina Manevska
articles.abstract: We draw on relational inequality theory (RIT) and status beliefs research to examine how social status shapes worker voice and supervisor responses to work-related issues. We investigate whether women, non-Western migrants, and lower-educated workers are less likely than men, native-born, and higher-educated workers to engage in claims-making by voicing concerns to their supervisor. Additionally, we examine whether supervisors are more likely to reject claims made by workers from lower-status groups. Using survey data (N = 3,215) from the Dutch labor market, we analyze status differences in worker voice behavior and perceived supervisor responses across workplaces. We find that workers with a non-Western migrant background or lower education are more likely to remain silent when experiencing a workplace issue, whereas gender differences in worker voice are explained by working hours. We find no evidence that lower-status workers report more suppression of their voice.

articles.title: Living off assets? European household incomes in the ‘asset economy’
articles.abstract: This study examines whether the expansion of asset ownership has given rise to ‘societies of petit rentiers’ shaped by generational differences in asset acquisition opportunities. Using the ECB Household Finance and Consumption Survey (2011–2021) covering up to 23 EU countries, we identify ‘petit-rentier’ households that derive at least 10% (and 20%) of total income from the ownership of rent-bearing assets. Together with descriptive statistics, we combine machine-learning feature selection with multilevel modelling to determine the main predictors of petit-rentier status. Our findings point to the continued dominance of traditional axes of inequality—class position and family wealth—albeit with an increasingly central role for real estate. Petit-rentier prevalence declines in most countries and asset-based income shifts towards real-estate rents. Non-worker households and multiple-property owners, rather than age cohort, show the strongest positive associations with petit-rentier status. The ‘asset economy’ appears to consolidate trajectories of income concentration rather than democratisation.

articles.title: Rising market power and its political discontents
articles.abstract: How does market power affect the political behavior of small business owners? As the growing market power of large multinational firms has fundamentally changed the opportunity structure for small businesses and their beneficiaries, we try to understand how those economic developments influence European democracies. We argue that growing market power lowers small business owners’ trust in key democratic institutions and the functioning of markets, driving them to reject incumbents and shift their support to radical right parties. We employ firm-level, individual-level, and regional-level data on fourteen European countries to test this argument. Our findings indicate that rising market power, measured by combining mergers and increases in market concentration, is associated with the declining economic performance of micro-firms. In turn, mergers and the declining economic share of these firms are robust predictors of anti-incumbent and increased radical right voting both at the individual and constituency levels. This article provides the first analysis of the effect of market concentration on rich democracies and, in doing so, offers a novel explanation for the surprising radical right support among small business owners in Europe.

articles.title: Peer-to-peer pressure? Social network-based opposition to cryptocurrency regulation
articles.abstract: This study examines whether peer influence shapes public attitudes toward cryptocurrency regulation among individuals without direct market exposure. While previous research has shown that participation in financial markets can foster regulatory skepticism, it remains unclear whether similar attitudinal shifts may emerge indirectly through interpersonal interaction. Drawing on three waves of panel survey data from Finland (2023–2025), the analysis investigates whether social proximity to cryptocurrency investors affects regulatory preferences among non-owners. Peer exposure is operationalized using three distinct components: the number of cryptocurrency-investing peers (passive influence), the frequency of cryptocurrency-related discussion (active influence), and perceived peer influence (receptiveness). Across dynamic ordered logit specifications incorporating lagged dependent variables and asset ownership fixed effects, the results indicate that discussion frequency is consistently associated with greater opposition to regulatory oversight. In contrast, passive exposure and self-reported receptiveness are not systematically related to regulatory attitudes once active interaction is accounted for.

articles.title: The role of collective ownership beliefs in shaping welfare chauvinism: experimental evidence from Türkiye’s dual welfare funding landscape
articles.abstract: Starting from the premise that public perceptions are endogenous to policy structures, this research examines how the interplay between policy funding schemes and identity differences affects public support for immigrant access to welfare assistance. It argues that collective proprietary claims over national resources are a key factor underpinning welfare chauvinism as natives seek to protect their exclusive entitlements within the national system. Leveraging Türkiye’s dual policy funding landscape, where foreign-aid-funded programs coexist with traditional welfare models, a population-representative survey experiment was conducted, differentiating between claimant identities and welfare assistance funding structures. The results show that the native–immigrant support gap emerges only when assistance is funded domestically but not through foreign aid. Moreover, solidarity for immigrants does not significantly increase when funding is switched from the state to foreign finance unless there are dire needs. The results carry implications for studies on welfare chauvinism and transnational migration governance.

articles.title: Public Opinion and the Political Logic of International Climate Pledges
articles.authors: Michaël Aklin, Mark T. Buntaine, Matto Mildenberger
articles.abstract: The 2015 Paris Agreement shifted the focus of global climate bargaining from collective, binding emissions reductions to regular, public, and unilateral climate pledges. These pledges reveal new information to the public about a government’s intended policies, bargaining approach, and responses to counterpart offers. We conducted three experiments across ten high-emitting countries with more than 10,000 respondents to examine whether the public becomes more supportive of climate action when observing conditional or unconditional public pledges. Domestic audiences prefer ambitious unilateral pledges over inaction. However, at high ambition levels, they favor conditional pledges emphasizing fairness between countries. Conditional pledges by counterpart countries do not increase support for domestic climate action, and they increase support for international transfers to low- and middle-income countries only when accompanied by ambitious unconditional pledges. Overall, conditional public pledging is insufficient to catalyze international cooperation by acting on public opinion.

articles.title: Don’t Fly Me to the Moon: A Moratorium on Lunar Industrialization
articles.abstract: A complex mix of geopolitical and commercial interests is accelerating plans for large-scale infrastructure development and resource extraction on the Moon. While the industrialization of the Moon may provide numerous economic benefits and facilitate further exploration of the solar system, it will likely cause adverse, irreversible impacts on the lunar environment and harmful knock-on effects on scientific research and cultural values. We suggest that there is a strong rationale and ample legal precedent for imposing a moratorium on lunar industrialization. As in other issue areas, a temporary prohibition could provide room for the development of robust international regulation, but also for broad and inclusive deliberation on the very desirability of lunar industrialization. The pace with which operational planning for lunar industrialization progresses suggests that there is an urgent need for governance interventions to safeguard the space environment and associated human values.

articles.title: Feminist Conservation: Politics and Power in Madagascar’s Marine Commons by Merrill Baker-Médard
Gateway Clubs: How ESG Indices Reinforce Transnational Voluntary Environmental Initiatives
articles.abstract: Many initiatives marshaling voluntary commitments to corporate sustainability have grown enormously through the inducement of reputational benefits and the partnership of NGOs and international organizations. Yet, as participants increasingly include less-than-ambitious companies, growth can nonetheless accelerate, even as it undermines the reputational distinction that membership originally offered. Why do initiatives then continue to draw new members? In this article, we advance a novel explanation: transnational environmental governance can become “embedded” in a parallel economic or political context such that joining “gateway clubs” becomes a means of ensuring access to external benefits. We demonstrate our argument with the case of the United Nations Global Compact (UNGC), where alignment with UNGC principles became a key criterion for inclusion in the S&P 500 ESG Index in January 2019. Using a difference-in-differences approach, our results suggest that US-domiciled companies eligible for S&P indexation were more likely to join and remain in the UNGC after January 2019.

articles.title: Who Shapes Air Pollution Governance? How Economic Development, Democracy, and Data Condition Stakeholder Influence in Six Majority World Cities
articles.authors: Ella Henninger, E. Keith Smith, Thomas Bernauer
articles.abstract: Air pollution is a major global health hazard, with the worst burden falling on cities in the Majority World. Yet which conditions shape governments’ willingness to act on air pollution remains poorly understood. Drawing on sixty-three semi structured interviews with seventy-two air pollution experts and stakeholders in six highly polluted cities (Accra, Kampala, Johannesburg, Jakarta, Dhaka, and Delhi), we examine how economic development, democracy, and data availability structure the influence of citizens, local advocates, economic elites, and country-external agencies on governments’ mitigation efforts. We find that governments remain primarily responsive to economic elites across levels of economic development, while external actors play a stronger role in the lowest-income case, Dhaka. Democracy strengthens citizens and local advocates through electoral accountability and civil society mobilization. Data availability creates opportunities for influence but also provokes governmental counter strategies. These findings highlight the centrality of stakeholder power in clean-air governance, showing how political, economic, and informational constraints shape whose demands governments respond to.

articles.title: How Information About Disaster Vulnerability Shapes Climate Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Talbot M. Andrews, Richard Clark, Rebecca Perlman
articles.abstract: Climate change is significantly increasing the frequency and severity of extreme weather events. Prior research indicates that exposure to such events can make individuals more supportive of green policies. But we know less about how this shapes individuals’ priorities across policies. Given that governments are budget constrained, policymakers may confront a trade-off between climate policy goals. We conducted original survey experiments in the United States to understand how information about climate vulnerability shapes preferences for adaptation and mitigation, particularly when voters are forced to choose between the two. We find that when individuals with weak priors are told about their vulnerability to extreme weather events, they prioritize local adaptation relative to mitigation, while those with stronger priors remain largely unmoved. Effects are especially consistent among independents, a crucial voting bloc as climate change becomes polarized. These findings underscore a potential challenge of mobilizing support for mitigation in cases in which mitigation and adaptation compete for funding.

articles.title: One Message, Multiple Functions: Local Propaganda as Bureaucratic Trace Management
articles.abstract: This article explores how local government propaganda in China can function as a tool for bureaucratic management. I argue that certain propaganda primarily serves as public documentation of government activities and officials’ performance, enhancing bureaucratic transparency and credibility. This documentation is particularly important when leaders lack personal ties with subordinates and thus require independent verification of their work. However, prioritizing record keeping over public persuasion often produces rigid, unengaging media content, which I term “trace-management propaganda.” Analyzing 1.4 million WeChat posts from Chinese local governments, I demonstrate that trace-management propaganda significantly increases during official evaluation periods and is especially prevalent where personal connections between leaders and subordinates are weak. A difference-in-differences analysis further confirms that a lack of personal ties increases reliance on trace-management propaganda. These findings reveal that local government propaganda in China frequently fulfills both administrative and expressive purposes, providing new insights into state media dynamics and bureaucratic oversight.

articles.title: Russia’s War on Ukraine: The Four Roots of Putin’s Invasion. By Taras Kuzio and Michał Wawrzonek. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 395p.
How Do Voters Reason about Intraparty Democracy? Constraints Rather than Influence
articles.abstract: Widespread intraparty reforms empower party members and create coprincipalship with party voters. This alters the structure of democratic delegation and may lead to policy drift and ineffective accountability. Existing research is vague on how voters see this arrangement, and we therefore ask, What leads voters to accept coprincipalship despite its potential representational costs? We apply exploratory analysis to focus-group data to examine how voters reason about intraparty authority and show that participants accepted their role as coprincipals not for self-empowerment, but for parties’ organizational integrity: they viewed party members as effective constraints on self-serving leaders. Based on these findings, we formulate an intraparty constraint hypothesis stating that voters favor intraparty democracy as a constraint mechanism rather than a participatory venue, which provides a theoretical answer to the unsolved puzzle of why voters want intraparty democracy when they do not intend to use it or reward parties for having it.

articles.title: Macroeconomic Implications of Executive Pay Caps,
articles.abstract: I study the introduction of statutory caps on executive pay ratios (pay caps) in a span-of-control economy with heterogeneous managerial talent. Managers hire fewer workers than they would in the absence of pay caps, and the marginal product of labour is not equalized among firms. The ability of the marginal manager declines. Inequality between managers and workers, and among managers, declines, but inequality among workers increases. Quantitatively, overall inequality decreases substantially, especially via a reduction in top income shares, but the GDP losses are also significant. In addition, the redistribution favours the “middle” deciles between 50 and 90, rather than the bottom 50% of the income distribution. Future work will build on this “first pass” to analyse the effect of pay caps in economies distorted by monopsony power, non-pecuniary benefits of control, and managerial rent extraction.

articles.title: Settled or Unsettled? Linking Migration Trajectories From Adolescence to Young Adulthood and Their Social Correlates in the United Kingdom
articles.abstract: Early‐life migration can shape subsequent migration, but how migration patterns in young adulthood resemble or differ from those in adolescence remains unclear. This study examines cross‐phase migration trajectory linkedness between adolescence (ages 13–17) and young adulthood (ages 21–25), and the social conditions under which such linkedness takes different forms. Using the British Household Panel Survey and its successor, Understanding Society ( N = 478), we construct annual migration sequences incorporating frequency, timing and distance, and quantify their resemblance using dyadic sequence analysis. The analysis identifies both resemblance and contrast in cross‐phase linkedness between adolescent and young‐adult migration. Resemblance is dominated by sustained immobility across both life phases, whereas contrast reflects divergence between the two phases, most often from immobility in adolescence to mobility in young adulthood. Regression analyses suggest that early marriage is associated with a lower likelihood of sustained immobility across both phases, whereas adolescent residence in London–South East is associated with a higher likelihood of this pattern. Being female and living in owner‐occupied housing during adolescence are both associated with the pattern of an immobile adolescence followed by a mobile young adulthood. The main findings are broadly robust to alternative classification schemes. Together, these trajectory‐level patterns caution against assuming that changes in mobility at one life stage translate uniformly into longer‐term internal migration trends.

articles.title: Anticipating Denied Futures: Temporalities of Protracted Refuge Among Congolese in Kampala
articles.abstract: This article develops a temporal perspective on protracted displacement by analysing the experiences of Congolese refugees in Kampala. It argues that displacement is both a spatial and a temporal condition, in which asylum and resettlement regimes are experienced as dispossessing refugees of their capacity to orient themselves toward the future. Drawing on longitudinal ethnographic research (2013–2025), the study traces the shift from initial expectations of rapid resettlement—imagined as a linear trajectory from Congo to Uganda to the Global North—to what many describe as a “life without a future.” This form of temporal dispossession shows how humanitarian and state regimes are experienced as governing not only mobility, but also refugees' capacity to imagine and inhabit the future. The article makes two main contributions to debates in migration and displacement studies. First, it contributes to the temporal turn in migration studies by distinguishing denied futurity from “waiting”: the collapse of future imaginaries reveals a condition in which waiting itself becomes difficult to sustain. Second, it highlights the ambivalent role of Pentecostal and Charismatic Christianity as a key arena of temporal reorientation. Religious narratives of “God's plan” reinstate teleology and sustain traces of futurity, while also functioning as vernacular critiques of humanitarian failure; yet they may simultaneously reproduce forms of deferred hope. Ultimately, the article demonstrates that time is a key terrain of governance, dispossession, and contestation in protracted displacement. By foregrounding the ambivalent role of faith, it shows how Congolese refugees negotiate temporal agency when institutional pathways have foreclosed the future.

articles.title: Escalators, not Equalisers: Core‐City Premiums in Intergenerational Social Mobility in China
articles.authors: Yiyue Huangfu, Haiyan Hao, Hongli Liang
articles.abstract: Do large cities promote intergenerational mobility? Existing evidence comes almost exclusively from developed societies, where urbanisation largely preceded metropolitan concentration. In rapidly developing contexts, these two processes unfold together, making it unclear whether large cities confer mobility advantages beyond urbanisation itself. This study disentangles these forces using pooled data from the 2014, 2016 and 2018 China Labour‐force Dynamics Survey. Comparing intergenerational occupational mobility across rural areas, non‐core cities, and core cities, defined as municipalities, provincial capitals, and sub‐provincial cities, we find a metropolitan mobility premium in absolute terms. In China, core‐city residence is associated with substantially higher absolute mobility (an escalator effect) but does not weaken intergenerational persistence (no equaliser effect). This escalator premium is evident among rural‐origin migrants, the in‐situ urbanised, and urban locals, is smaller and not statistically significant among urban‐origin migrants, and is largely attenuated after accounting for educational attainment and hukou incorporation. These findings caution against equating rising mobility with expanding equality of opportunity. In developing contexts, large cities may accelerate structural upgrading while leaving the intergenerational transmission of advantage intact.

articles.title: Deliberating international politics: Listening and consensus-orientation in the United Nations Security Council
articles.authors: Gisela Hirschmann, Monika Heupel, Evgenija Kröker
articles.abstract: The United Nations Security Council (UNSC) is typically seen as a forum in which states engage in bargaining: Powerful states pressure others to vote in their favor, and weaker states go along with this in exchange for support on other issues. We complement this view by redirecting the analytical lens from voting outcomes to the discursive processes that shape them. We argue that UNSC members also engage in deliberative behavior – specifically, listening and consensus-orientation – to foster cooperative solutions. We suggest that variation in deliberative practices can be explained by selected debate- and speaker-related factors. To test our claims, we analyze 27,812 speeches from UNSC meetings between 1995 and 2020, using a custom dictionary to identify deliberative cues, and corroborate our findings through six interviews with current and former UNSC members. We show that listening and consensus-orientation are indeed central to UNSC debates but vary based on the timing and format of a debate, the contestedness of the issue, and the economic wealth of a speaker’s country. This article calls on scholars to take deliberative behavior in the study of UNSC politics seriously to develop a more comprehensive understanding of international cooperation.

articles.title: From Public to Private Governance, and Back—Eco‐Modulation as De‐Privatization in Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)
articles.authors: Harri Kalimo, Antti Jukka, Reid Lifset, Petrus Kautto
articles.abstract: The European Union is advancing circular economy policies, aimed at reducing the environmental impacts of products across their life‐cycles. Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) exemplifies this strategy. It privatizes the end‐of‐life management of products to their producers, seeking thereby to incentivize the producer to design environmentally more sustainable products. However, EPR has failed to deliver significant improvements in product design. This article examines the EU's attempts to strengthen eco‐design in EPR through ‘eco‐modulation’. Applying the theory of competence‐and‐control, the article argues that the introduction of eco‐modulation will destabilize the public‐private balance in EPR, shifting EPR back from private towards public governance. This de‐privatization is expected to refine EPR's role within the EU's policy mix. Our findings thus offer insights for the development of EPR‐related circular economy policies, while also contributing to theories of privatization.

articles.title: Regulatory Learning or Regulatory Privilege? How Sandbox Design Shapes the Governance Value of Experimental Regulation
articles.abstract: Regulatory sandboxes are controlled, time‐limited environments in which selected innovations are tested under regulatory supervision. This article asks how sandbox design can make selective experimentation capable of generating public regulatory value rather than regulatory privilege. It develops regulatory learning asymmetry to distinguish private, supervisory, and public regulatory learning and unequal distributions of access, information, learning, and benefits. A structured reading of public documents from five deliberately diverse FinTech and artificial intelligence cases illustrates a six‐element operational framework. The case material is not used to infer private or supervisory learning; it records only publication, generalization mechanisms, and documented uptake. The framework identifies a public‐learning configuration, a supervisory‐learning configuration that public documents cannot verify, and a regulatory‐privilege risk configuration. Market signaling is treated as a cross‐cutting dynamic. The article offers a bounded diagnostic for assessing whether case‐specific experience becomes contestable and institutionally usable knowledge.

Soil Degradation in Sub-Saharan Agriculture
articles.authors: Julia Berazneva, David Güereña, Annemie Maertens, Hope C. Michelson
articles.abstract: Soil degradation poses a critical challenge to food security, poverty reduction, and sustainable development in Sub-Saharan Africa. In this review, we synthesize economic perspectives on soil degradation in Sub-Saharan Africa. We draw on concepts, measures, and analysis from the biophysical sciences to define soil degradation and present evidence of its extent. We review the drivers of soil degradation and its economic consequences and indicate possible approaches toward remediation. We highlight opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration to jointly address soil health and rural welfare.

articles.title: Robert S. Pindyck: Real Options, Optimal Control, and the Pedagogical Legacy of Uncertainty
articles.abstract: Robert S. Pindyck, who is the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi Professor in Finance and Economics as well as a professor of applied economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), has shaped how economists and policymakers analyze investment, energy markets, and climate policy under uncertainty. Beginning with early work in dynamic optimization, he helped migrate option-pricing logic from finance into the economics of “real” decisions (such as entry, exit, and capacity choice) via the real options program developed with Saman Majd and Avinash Dixit. In energy and natural resources, Pindyck's models and empirics clarified interfuel substitution, storage and inventory dynamics, and cartel behavior. In climate economics, he became a prominent critic of the overprecision of integrated assessment models (IAMs), proposing decision frameworks that emphasize deep uncertainty and tail risk while arguing for robust carbon pricing. Equally important is his pedagogical legacy: with Daniel Rubinfeld, Pindyck coauthored two widely used textbooks ( Microeconomics and Econometric Models and Economic Forecasts ) that trained generations in rigorous modeling, identification, forecasting, and market analysis. This article synthesizes his career and research arc, contrasts the Dixit–Pindyck real options approach with the Fisher–Arrow–Henry tradition of quasi-option value, reviews his energy and climate policy contributions, and highlights his influence as a teacher and econometric innovator.

China's Climate Policies: Climate Targets and Implementation Mechanisms
articles.authors: Yazhen Gong, Min Wang, Jinhua Zhao
articles.abstract: China leads the world in both greenhouse gas emissions and renewable energy deployment. In recent years, China has committed to increasingly ambitious climate goals and is on track to meeting these goals. This article provides a systematic review of China's climate policies and their impacts. We argue that China's climate policies can be classified into two components: binding climate-related targets and a mixture of command-and-control and market-based implementation mechanisms. We discuss how the mechanisms have performed and the lessons they offer for the future climate policies of China and other countries.

articles.title: Current State of Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage Technologies
articles.authors: Yanyou Guan, Gordon Rausser, David Zilberman
articles.abstract: Addressing climate change requires significant efforts toward decarbonization. This review provides a comprehensive technical, economic, and policy assessment of 239 carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technologies. Categorizing pathways by application and physicochemical processes, we evaluate technological maturity using Technology Readiness Levels and economic viability via capture costs and the impact of capture on product price. Findings indicate that CCUS technologies are heterogeneous; most currently remain immature and face prohibitive costs, trapping private capital in a wait-and-see dynamic driven by severe risk premiums and externalities. To overcome these market failures, we advocate for a hybrid public-private framework: utilizing early-stage public funding to derisk development and catalyze learning-by-doing, subsequently transitioning to robust carbon pricing mechanisms. Furthermore, we highlight the critical role of international coordination in resolving systemic challenges associated with global externalities, spatial heterogeneity, and the fragmentation of markets, supply chains, and regulatory regimes.

articles.title: Algorithmic Literacy and Quotidian Curation Practices: Rethinking User Agency in the Social Media Regulation Era
articles.abstract: This paper examines the practices ordinary social media users employ to influence the content served to them by platform algorithms, and the relationship between these practices and levels of algorithmic literacy. Practices were documented across TikTok, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter (now X), YouTube and Reddit during 65 sessions, conducted as part of a digital ethnographic study of Australian social media users aged 18–30. The paper presents a taxonomy of curation practices, categorised as active or passive, and inviting or dissuading of content. The diversity of practices used by participants in the study points to a degree of user agency, exercised within proprietary algorithmic content systems, not previously explored in the literature. In the context of rising public concern about the harms of social media use, particularly to young people, and policy responses that focus on restricting access to social media, this paper offers a more nuanced account of user experiences online, foregrounding their agency, practical expertise and capacity to deploy protective strategies when engaging with algorithmically mediated content flows.

articles.title: The WorkReach model for urban work location choices through economic complexity and informality
articles.authors: Ollin D. Langle-Chimal, Steffen Knoblauch, Marta C. González
articles.abstract: Human mobility in urban areas largely depends on the spatial distribution of jobs and who pursues them, yet how workers balance proximity against economic opportunity remains poorly understood. Existing mechanistic models capture physically interpretable effects such as distance decay, but overlook how socioeconomic factors shape commuting decisions. We present WorkReach, a model grounded in discrete choice theory that embeds informality and economic complexity into a utility function and represents commuting as the outcome of workers behaving as if maximizing it. Applied to four cities in the United States, Mexico, and Brazil, it reproduces commuting flows as accurately as widely used benchmarks while making the underlying choices interpretable. Here, we show that workers consistently commute farther to economically sophisticated areas, while the role of informality differs across regions, and that measuring accessibility by the perceived benefit of opportunities, not just physical proximity, highlights disparities conventional metrics overlook.

articles.title: Emergence of polarization in networks of large language model agents
articles.authors: Jinghua Piao, Zhihong Lu, Chen Gao, Fengli Xu, Qinghua Hu, Fernando P. Santos, Yong Li, James Evans
articles.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have empowered autonomous agents to generate social networks, communicate, and form shared and diverging opinions on political issues. However, our understanding of their collective behaviours and underlying mechanisms remains incomplete. In this paper, we simulate networked systems involving thousands of LLM agents across different backbone models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, ChatGLM, Llama-3, and DeepSeek-V3), in which agents interact through LLM-guided conversations and update their opinions over time, resulting in the emergence of opinion polarization. We discover that these agents spontaneously develop their own social network with properties characteristic of human social networks, such as homophilic clustering. The collective opinions of these LLM agents evolve in ways that exhibit behavioural patterns consistent with social phenomena and mechanisms widely discussed in empirical studies of human behaviour and opinion-dynamics models. This consistency suggests that LLM agents can serve as a valuable synthetic testbed for exploring hypothetical intervention strategies in networked LLM-agent systems. Using this testbed, we further examine the effects of a range of network- and individual-level interventions, such as promoting more diverse interactions and reducing confirmation bias. Overall, this work not only sheds light on subtle opinion dynamics and collective behaviour of LLM agents from a network perspective, but also demonstrates their potential for testing hypotheses about opinion dynamics and intervention strategies.

articles.title: “We need the right kind of people in this neighborhood”: racial motivation in opposition to new housing construction
articles.abstract: How we measure racial bias matters. Previous literature demonstrates that direct questioning leads to unreliable responses. Scholars have thus developed a number of techniques to uncover racial bias without cuing a defensive response. I investigate the performance of text- and image-based factorial experiments in the case of racial motivation for opposition to new housing development relative to a more traditional list experiment. My results demonstrate that these often-used methods yield substantially different conclusions about the importance of racial biases in opposition to new housing construction. While the factorial experiments suggest little evidence of racial bias, the more traditional list experiment reveals that the potential for racial change in their neighborhood is a concern for a meaningful share of respondents.

articles.title: Carneiro’s global dataset of cultural traits in ethnographic and historical societies: a digital edition
articles.authors: Václav Hrnčíř, Robert Forkel, Russell D. Gray
articles.abstract: The late Robert L. Carneiro was a prominent anthropologist who devoted his life to the study of political evolution and the evolution of complex societies. In the 1960s and 1970s, he and his colleagues created a cross-cultural dataset for their Scale Analysis project, collecting ethnographic and historical data on hundreds of cultural traits in more than a hundred societies worldwide. Although Carneiro presented the results of the project in several papers, the dataset itself has not yet been published. Here we present a digital version of two editions of the dataset, based on Carneiro’s documentation stored in the archives of the American Museum of Natural History. The 4th edition contains 127 societies and 354 cultural traits, and the 6th edition features 74 societies and 618 traits. Both represent unique sets of coded cross-cultural information that can be used as a comparative source to other cross-cultural datasets, as a starting point for one’s own collection of cross-cultural data, and for quantitative testing of cultural evolutionary hypotheses.

articles.title: Seeing Is Believing? Most People Struggle to Detect AI-Generated Images
articles.authors: Mads Fuglsang Hove, Frederik Hjorth, Yevgeniy Golovchenko, Rebecca Adler-Nissen, Anja Bechmann, Arjen van Dalen, Sara B. Hobolt, Claes de Vreese
articles.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) dramatically lowers the costs of creating high-quality, realistic images, allowing a wider range of actors to create and distribute such content on, for instance, social media. A core concern is that easy-to-use generative AI tools can be misused for manipulation through misinformation and microtargeted persuasive material. However, we still need more contextual nuance to a fundamental question: To what degree can people discern photorealistic AI-generated images from authentic images? In a preregistered survey experiment, we find that, on average, people are not substantially better than chance at discerning AI-generated images from authentic images, regardless of the context of the image. While younger people, highly analytical-thinking individuals, and experienced users of generative AI have better discernment abilities, no demographic group other than young individuals (<25) performs substantially better than chance. Contrary to our expectation, we do not find that people’s confidence in their discernment abilities varies depending on the context of the image. As generative AI technology likely advances and the realism of AI-generated images continues to improve, these findings are concerning, as people already struggle to discern between AI-generated and authentic images, even in an experiment where they have been primed and are assessing images of relatively low quality.

The politics of categorizing people of african descent - global frameworks, political meanings, and shifting boundaries of belonging
articles.abstract: The article examines how the United Nations (UN) politically creates and structures the category “people of African descent” (PAD). It shows that, in international political debates, this category is closely linked to migration-related categories but not necessarily solely through overlaps, but also through processes of differentiation that further complicate the categorization process. Through a qualitative analysis this article examines the relationship between the category of ‘migrant’ and the ‘people of African descent’. It shows that the two are closely linked: Migration functions both as an internal mechanism of differentiation and as a demarcation from other migrant groups. At the same time, 'migrant itself is not a uniform category, but is constantly redefined in conjunction with race, legal status, gender and generation. This creates a complex political grammar in which the intertwining of people of African descent and migration marks specific forms of discrimination, vulnerability and visibility in the UN discourse.

articles.title: Uninstitutionalized regional integration: a comparative analysis of migration governance and migrant integration in the Organization of Turkic States
articles.authors: Barış Demirel, Fatma Rümeysa Taşbaş, Ömer Faruk Cantekin
articles.abstract: This study comparatively examines the level and patterns of institutionalization of migrant integration in the member countries of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS). Focusing on Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, and Türkiye, the study investigates how integration is positioned across different policy areas and discusses the governance dynamics that may explain the observed institutionalization patterns. The study is based on directed content analysis of national legislation and policy documents that were in force or constituted the relevant policy framework during the 2010–2026 study period, supplemented by OTS and international organization documents used for contextual analysis. The eight policy areas of MIPEX were used as the analytical reference framework, and the intensity of integration institutionalization was comparatively assessed through a qualitative evaluation framework based on normative recognition, administrative mechanisms, and rights-based scope. The findings show that integration policies are relatively more visible, particularly in the area of labor market access; however, institutional intensity remains lower in areas such as political participation, long-term residency, and combating discrimination. This suggests that integration is positioned not as an autonomous multidimensional membership regime, but rather as a complementary element of regulatory and economically focused migration management. The study interprets this pattern in relation to a governance logic formed by the intersection of the assumption of transience, security-based governance, and economic instrumentalization, and proposes the concept of “uninstitutionalized regional integration” as an original contribution to the migration governance literature. The findings suggest that the institutionalization of integration is shaped not only by migration intensity or administrative capacity, but also by governance rationalities that define migrants’ position within the political and social order.

Crisis, segmentation, and immigrant labor market incorporation: COVID-19 in the U.S. restaurant industry
articles.authors: Ernesto F. L. Amaral, Huyen Pham, Raymond Robertson, Suojin Wang, Nereyda Y. Ortiz Osejo de Lemus
articles.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic generated an unprecedented labor market shock that disproportionately affected face-to-face service sectors central to immigrant employment. This study examines whether the pandemic reaffirmed or revealed limits to the narrative of immigrant resilience that emerged from research on the Great Recession. Focusing on the U.S. restaurant industry (a large, low-wage, nontraded sector with high immigrant representation), we analyze differential employment trajectories of foreign-born and U.S.-born workers across contraction and recovery phases. We integrate three data sources: 2000–2022 CPS Annual Social and Economic Supplement data to establish long-term occupational trends; longitudinal CPS Basic Monthly data to estimate worker transitions during the pandemic; and an original nationwide survey of restaurant owners and hiring managers conducted in Summer 2021 with retrospective staffing information for January 2020 and January 2021. CPS transition results indicate that foreign-born workers experienced sharper transitions into unemployment in certain occupational segments during the contraction phase. Employer survey results suggest that foreign-born workers became increasingly concentrated in lower-wage restaurant types during recovery. These findings suggest that the national scope and mobility-restricting nature of COVID-19 constrained traditional immigrant adjustment mechanisms. Rather than uniformly reinforcing immigrant resilience, the pandemic intensified intra-industry segmentation and revealed how crisis characteristics condition immigrant labor market incorporation.

articles.title: Psychological and computational evidence that merit is a constructed evaluative process
articles.abstract: Merit is a foundational moral principle invoked to justify inequality between people, yet an individual’s productivity is shaped not only by their efforts but also their opportunities. How, then, do people construct merit judgements? Across four preregistered, incentivized studies with US-based samples (total N = 759), we provide psychological and computational evidence that merit is not the product of a fixed rule, but rather the outcome of a subjective valuation. In a two-stage paradigm, participants first completed a real-effort tournament that dissociated performance (effort) from structural productivity (output dependent on opportunity). Thereafter, groups of observers and stakeholders allocated resources to tournament players. Across studies, a player’s performance and structural productivity influenced how people judged deservingness. Computational modeling revealed that decision-makers integrated these dimensions of merit into a value computation that shaped allocations. Crucially, individuals differed in their latent weighting patterns, yielding subgroups with directly opposing conceptions of deservingness. By revealing merit as a nonuniform ideal, these findings provide a mechanistic account of how deservingness is determined, helping explain the compelling yet contested nature of meritocracy.

articles.title: Recreational screen use and internalizing problems from preadolescence to young adulthood in a longitudinal twin cohort with co-twin comparison
articles.authors: Tong Gong, Emma Frans, Anna Ohlis, Shuyang Yao, Ruyue Zhang, Anders Nilsson, Yasmina Molero, Miriam A. Mosing, Isabell Brikell, Henrik Larsson, Paul Lichtenstein, Lisa B. Thorell, Patrik KE Magnusson, Ralf Kuja-Halkola, Yi Lu
articles.abstract: The mental health impact of increasing recreational screen use among youth has raised substantial concerns, yet questions about causality remain unresolved. Here, leveraging a co-twin control design, we examined associations between screen use and internalizing problems from childhood to early adulthood among 21,797 Swedish twins, accounting for shared familial factors. Recreational screen use was associated with increased internalizing symptoms and clinical diagnosed depression and anxiety. However, these associations were substantially attenuated within discordant twin pairs and did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. These findings suggest that shared genetic and environmental factors partly explain the association between youth screen use and mental health. Although co-twin estimates provided limited evidence for clear causal effects, the association between heavy interactive screen use and clinical risk highlights the need to understand potential mechanisms linking digital behaviours and youth mental health.
